chunks.subject: AP Comparative Government
chunks.title: Q3 Comparative Analysis (5 points) — Set 1: judicial systems
chunks.content: AP Comparative Government FRQ 3 is Comparative Analysis, 5 points: A describe a concept (1), B describe/apply it in TWO different AP Comparative course countries (2, one per country), C explain WHY for each of those two countries (2, one per country). The six course countries are China, Iran, Mexico, Nigeria, Russia, and the UK. Set 1 answer key: A [1] a function of a judicial system (interpret laws, assess constitutionality, resolve disputes, apply law, checks and balances, protect rights, establish rule of law). B [2] describe a limit on judicial power in two course countries (e.g., China: judiciary under CCP control / rule by law; Russia: judges nominated by the President, no judicial review; UK: no judicial review, bound by common law; Iran: Chief Justice appointed by Supreme Leader). C [2] explain why each country limits judicial power (e.g., China/Russia: executive consolidates power / controls dissent; UK: parliamentary sovereignty / prevent any branch dominating; Mexico/Nigeria: checks and balances). Common failure: attributing powers a country's executive does not actually have; explanations that restate the limit rather than give a reason. Both B and C are country-specific — an inaccurate country claim loses that country's point in both.

chunks.subject: AP Comparative Government
chunks.title: Q3 Set 1 exemplar — Sample 3A, 5/5
chunks.content: Q3 (Set 1) scored 5/5. A: judicial function = resolve civil and criminal disputes. B (both earned): UK lacks judicial review (cannot rule on constitutionality of Parliament's laws); Russia's judiciary lacks independence, judges nominated by the President. C (both earned): UK limits the judiciary to concentrate power in Parliament/executive and preserve policy continuity; Russia limits it so the executive (Putin) can consolidate power. Full-credit model with accurate, country-specific claims.

chunks.subject: AP Comparative Government
chunks.title: Q3 Set 1 exemplar — Sample 3B, 3/5
chunks.content: Q3 (Set 1) scored 3/5. A: judicial review of laws' constitutionality. B: 1/2 — UK point earned (advises Parliament via committees but cannot overturn laws); Russia point lost (incorrectly said Russia's judiciary 'doesn't have judicial review'). C: 1/2 — UK explanation lost (efficiency claim didn't clarify parliamentary sovereignty); Russia earned (limits judiciary so United Russia keeps one-party dominance and Putin consolidates power). Shows how one inaccurate country claim costs a point while the parallel country still scores.

chunks.subject: AP Comparative Government
chunks.title: Q3 Set 1 exemplar — Sample 3C, 1/5
chunks.content: Q3 (Set 1) scored 1/5. Earned only A (judiciary checks laws against the constitution). Lost both B points and both C points because it attributed powers the executives do not possess — claimed Nigeria's president can remove justices and Mexico's president can ignore judicial rulings. Illustrates that factually wrong country claims void both the description and explanation points for those countries.
